newsitem.title: USA: Orange County, Calif., board considers debt plan.
newsitem.headline: Orange County, Calif., board considers debt plan.

text.p: Orange County, Calif., supervisors on Tuesday will consider a plan that would reduce county debt levels to "build trust" on Wall Street in the wake of its bankruptcy.

The county's chief financial officer, Gary Burton, proposed the "Credit and Debt Management" plan last month. It calls for the refinancing of county bonds and for the county to build up its budget reserves.
Under Burton's plan, the county would build up its year-end fund balances, using a portion of the extra revenues to defease or retire bonds before maturity.

Burton said the county should be able to build up a $140 million fund balance by fiscal 2001-2002. Those funds could be used to retire county bonds. The county could also defease bonds gradually, between now and 2002, Burton said.
By refinancing its 1995 Teeter bonds, Burton said the county would free up reserves and could save about $5 million annually in the coming years.

Burton said his program could reduce county debt per capita to $482 from $572. General obligation and lease debt as a percentage of assessed valuation would drop to 0.70 percent from 0.85 percent, he said.
Burton said his program could help the county attain single-A debt ratings and would ensure it pays less on future borrowings.
"We're trying to build trust with Wall Street, Main Street and Sacramento," Burton said.
Burton said he expected the Board of Supervisors to approve his plan at Tuesday's meeting.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. It emerged from bankruptcy last June.
